chapters.title: Chapter 1: Flowers and Nets
chapters.html:
Mydei never really understood what his father expected of him when he sent him away from Castrum Kremnos. The whole thing had unfolded too quickly, like a decision made long before anyone bothered to tell him.

“Your reputation is not great, Mydeimos,” King Eurypon had said, fingers steepled, voice infuriatingly calm. “People are wary of you. They think you’ll start a war the moment someone looks at you wrong. They see your temper…”, he hesitated, choosing the right words, “...and they do not like it.” 

Mydei had barked a laugh at that, low and sharp.
“And Your Majesty thought kicking me out was the best idea?” he’d snickered, crossing his arms as if shielding himself from the sting beneath the joke.

Gorgo had tried to interject then, stepping between father and son like she always did, but even her patience couldn’t soften Eurypon’s decision. The king’s mind was sealed long before the conversation began.

So three days later, Mydei packed his things in a silence that settled like dust over everything he touched. He said his goodbyes to the few people who mattered —family, friends, the rare souls who didn’t flinch at his presence— and tried not to think too hard about the fact that this felt more like exile than guidance.

At dawn, he mounted his horse and left the capital behind, riding south towards Aedes Elysiae, a tiny village tucked at the very edge of Amphoreus. Rumor said it was peaceful. 

Mydei wasn’t sure if that was supposed to comfort him or punish him, since he was not used to staying still. Stillness left too much room for thought, and he preferred his mind occupied with motion, strategy, anything but the echo of his own doubts.

While passing by the first stretch of open fields, Mydei loosened his grip on the reins, letting his shoulders ease for the first time since the argument. Golden grasses swayed in slow waves, brushing against one another with the soft hiss of wind over silk. The sky here was wider than it ever felt within the walls of the capital and, for a brief, quiet moment, he allowed himself to breathe.

He believed his father meant well with all of this. Eurypon wasn’t cruel; just impossibly stubborn, convinced that distance would temper his son’s rough edges. And maybe a village where nothing ever happened would smooth him into something less sharp.

But Mydei couldn’t pinpoint why he felt this strange tug in his chest —something between resentment and longing, as if he were leaving behind more than just stone walls and familiar faces; as if he were being pushed toward something he wasn’t ready to name.

The road stretched ahead, long and empty. With every step his horse took, the capital slipped farther from view, and the quiet of the countryside grew heavier, almost expectant.

He wondered what waited for him in Aedes Elysiae, but before he even got to form a thought, something slammed into the side of his horse with a dull thud.

Mydei swore, jerking the reins as the startled animal danced sideways. Instinct had him shifting his weight and reaching back for the long spear strapped to his saddle, only to find a man on the ground, tangled in a mess of fishing nets and wildflowers, blinking up at him like he was the one who had been ridden over.

“Titans above, sorry!” the stranger sputtered, pushing himself upright. His silver hair was messy, and his clothes were damp as though he’d crawled out of the riverside. “Didn’t think anyone actually used this road in the morning…”

Mydei cut him off with a scowl. “Didn’t think anyone would be lying in the middle of it.”

The stranger laughed as if nearly getting trampled was a charming inconvenience. “Wasn’t lying. I was… ambushed.”

“By what? A net you threw yourself into?” Mydei deadpanned.

“By gravity,” the man said proudly, as though it were an acceptable answer. He brushed dirt off his tunic and offered a grin that was far too bright for this hour of the morning. “Name’s Phainon.”

Mydei raised a brow but didn’t offer his own name. Instead, he looked the man up and down —the nets, the muddy boots, the confident stance that didn’t match the disaster he’d just witnessed.

“You always greet travelers by launching yourself at their horses?” Mydei asked.

“Only the interesting ones,” Phainon shot back, hands on his hips while smiling wildly. Mydei felt a flicker of something. Whether it was annoyance or curiosity, he couldn’t tell. 

Phainon squinted at him, as though assessing him right back. “You’re headed south, right? Toward Aedes Elysiae?”

Mydei frowned. “And if I am?”

“Then I’m going the same way.” Phainon’s grin turned competitive, sharp around the edges. “Race you to the next bend?”

Mydei snorted. “On foot? You’d lose.”

“Maybe,” Phainon said with a grin, “but I still plan on giving you a chase.”

He said it with such confidence that Mydei felt his own competitive streak shift awake, stretching like a cat ready to pounce.

“Fine,” Mydei said. “Try to keep up.”

“Oh, I intend to,” Phainon said, and Mydei had the strange, unwelcome feeling the man wasn’t just talking about the road.

Phainon didn’t wait for Mydei to give a proper signal. The moment the words left Mydei’s mouth, Phainon spun on his heel and shot off down the dirt path with the chaotic enthusiasm of someone who absolutely did not think this through.

Mydei blinked.

“…He’s actually running.”

For a heartbeat, he just stared at the absurd sight of the man sprinting ahead —nets still half-draped over one shoulder, hair bouncing, laughing like the whole world was an inside joke only he understood.

Then something in Mydei’s chest snapped.

Competitive instinct. Territory instinct. Pure spite instinct. Hard to tell.

With an exasperated exhale, he nudged his horse forward into an easy trot, not enough to barrel past Phainon, but enough to loom behind him, close enough that Phainon would feel it.

Phainon glanced back mid-run, eyes bright, breathless but still grinning.

“Oh, come on! That’s cheating!”

“You challenged someone on a horse,” Mydei pointed out dryly. “Sounds like a you problem.”

Phainon laughed a little breathless. “Then get off and run!”

Mydei raised a brow. “You really think you could outrun me?”

“No,” Phainon admitted, then added, “But I’d like to see you try.”

HKS.

Mydei swung off the saddle in one smooth motion and landed on the dirt with a quiet thud. Phainon’s eyes widened, surprise flickering into delight.

“Oh,” Phainon said, backing up a step as Mydei rolled his shoulders. “You’re serious.”

“You wanted a race,” Mydei said, tying his horse’s reins to a fencepost. “You’re getting a race.”

Phainon’s grin returned full force, bright enough to rival the morning sun. “All right then. First to the bend.”

Mydei stood beside him. “You sure you can handle losing?”

Phainon shot him a sideways look, breathing hard but smiling like he’d been waiting for someone to challenge him like this for a very long time.

“Lose? To you? Please. You sure have a conspicuous physique, but I’m betting you don’t have the speed to reach me.”

Mydei huffed a quiet laugh —more reaction than he intended to show.

They crouched slightly, the air between them tightening in anticipation.

“Ready?” Phainon asked.

Mydei smirked. “Try not to trip this time.”

“That was one time!”

Mydei didn’t have time to laugh, because Phainon bolted again. “You little—!” Mydei shot forward after him.

Their feet pounded the dirt path, gravel kicking up behind them. Phainon was fast but Mydei’s strides were longer, trained. They fell into a rhythm neither of them intended: Phainon darting ahead with reckless bursts of speed, Mydei closing the distance with predatory calm.

Halfway to the bend, Phainon called over his shoulder, breathless, “You really are terrifying!”

“And you talk too much,” Mydei shot back, gaining on him.

“Talking is a strategy!”

“For what? Losing faster?”

“For throwing you off!”

“It’s not working.”

“It is kind of working!”

“Shut up and run”, Mydei warned, a smile almost making it to his face.

They were so close enough now that Mydei could hear Phainon’s breath and under the rising sun, with wildflowers brushing their legs and the road stretching wide before them, Mydei realized he was enjoying this, which was kind of absurd.

Mydei closed the last bit of distance between them, matching Phainon’s pace stride for stride. Their arms brushed once, twice —each time accidental, followed by Phainon’s breathless, incredulous laugh.

“You…,” Phainon panted, “you are not allowed to be this fast! You’re cheating at running!”

“How?” Mydei asked, deadpan. “By moving my legs?”

“YES!”

Mydei rolled his eyes so hard he nearly stumbled.

The bend was close now, curving around a cluster of tall cypresses, sunlight splintering between them. Phainon dug deep, pushing himself into one last reckless burst of speed. Mydei matched it effortlessly, legs burning, blood pounding, lungs full of clean morning air that tasted almost sweet.

They hit the bend at the exact same moment. A pair of shadows converging, two sets of feet skidding in the dirt. Both of them ended up laughing, breathless but triumphant.

Phainon stumbled sideways into a patch of grass, hands on his knees as he gasped for air.

Mydei bent forward, palms braced on his thighs, chest rising and falling in heavy pulls. He wasn’t used to running for fun. He wasn’t used to laughing while he did it, either.

Phainon lifted his head, hair sticking to his forehead, grin wide and wild.
“Okay,” he wheezed. “Okay. That was… I haven’t run like that since… well, ever.”

Mydei swallowed a grin he didn’t mean to show. “You kept up,” he admitted.

Phainon blinked, stunned. Then he lit up like someone had just handed him a crown. “You saying that feels like winning.”

“It wasn’t a compliment.”

“It was absolutely a compliment.”

Mydei grunted, looking away.

They stood there a moment, catching their breaths, morning light settling soft and golden around them. Mydei felt… lighter. A little dizzy, but not from the run.

Phainon wiped his forehead with the back of his hand, still smiling. “So… Mysterious Horse Guy.”

Mydei stiffened. “Don’t call me that.”

“Then tell me your name.”

“No.”

Phainon blinked. “No?”

“That’s what I said.”

Phainon threw his hands into the air. “How am I supposed to keep calling you something? You’re clearly not going to answer to ‘Hey you.’”

“Try me.”

Phainon groaned loudly, flopping back into the grass. “Titans above, what kind of person refuses to share their name after a race like that?”

“The kind who didn’t ask for company.”

“C’mon,” Phainon scoffed. “If you didn’t want company, you wouldn’t have gotten off your horse.”

Mydei opened his mouth and closed it again. HKS.

Phainon sat up, brushing grass off his elbows. “Fine. If you won’t tell me, I’ll guess.”

“You won’t.”

“Oh? Watch me.” Phainon tapped his chin thoughtfully. “Hmm… You look like a—”

“No.”

“You don’t even know what I was going to say!”

“I know it would’ve been wrong.”

“Okay, but let me try at least one!”

Mydei crossed his arms. “No.”

“I’m not leaving this bend until you tell me your name.”

“Enjoy living here, then.”

Phainon gaped at him for a full two seconds and then burst out laughing. “You’re impossible.”

Mydei shrugged. “And you’re persistent.”

“That’s basically the same thing.”

“It’s not.”

“It’s not?”

Mydei felt a laugh tug at his chest again. He exhaled instead, steadying himself.

Phainon leaned toward him, grin softening but eyes still mischievous. “Come on, you already know mine. It’s only fair.”

Mydei hesitated. He thought of his father, of Gorgo, of guards and councilmen and the whispering citizens who recoiled at his shadow.

He thought of Phainon’s carefree and unguarded laughter.

He didn’t want that to change.

“…I’ll tell you someday,” he said finally.

Phainon blinked slowly, and all of a sudden a smile spread across his face —not teasing, but gentle. “Someday, huh?”

Mydei didn’t meet his eyes. “If you stop asking.”

“Not a chance.”

Mydei groaned. Phainon beamed.

They stood there, side by side, the quiet morning settling around them like a warm cloak. Mydei’s horse neighed impatiently from behind the bend, and Phainon perked up.

“Come on, Mystery Guy,” he said, already heading back toward the road. “We’ve got a village to reach.”

“Do not call me that.”

However, Mydei still followed him, slow but steady, wondering how a complete stranger had managed to wedge himself so firmly into his day.

Phainon glanced back once, walking backward with no sense of self-preservation. “You’ll tell me eventually,” he said, winking.

Mydei felt heat rise behind his ribs.

“We’ll see,” he muttered.

They reached the road again, the bend now behind them, the run lingering in their lungs and legs like a shared secret neither quite knew how to name.

Phainon led the way, humming some uneven tune as he walked. Mydei followed with his horse at his side, watching the strange man ahead of him kick stones, tug leaves off bushes, and almost trip twice while doing both. The quiet between them wasn’t awkward. It was… oddly companionable.

“Where exactly are we going?” Mydei finally asked.

Phainon pointed ahead without looking back. “My place.”

Mydei frowned. “Your…?”

He grinned over his shoulder. “Try not to be impressed.”

“I’m not.”

“You will be.”

Mydei snorted softly but said nothing.

They reached the farmhouse just as the sun climbed higher, golden light spilling across the stone walls and tangled vines. The sheep wandered lazily nearby, unbothered by their arrival. Phainon stopped at the edge of the porch, chest heaving, grin still wild and a little triumphant.

“Welcome,” he said, spreading his arms as though presenting a castle rather than a modest home. “To the incredible, slightly crooked, entirely glorious Phainon’s farm.”

Mydei’s eyes swept over it all: the sun-bleached wood, the curling vines, the uneven stones of the porch, the smell of warm earth and something sweet he couldn’t name. For a moment, he just… stood there.

It wasn’t the capital. There were no polished floors, no grand halls, no wary courtiers whispering behind fans. There was only light, air, and the quiet hum of life.

Phainon nudged him gently. “Come on. I mean it, you can stay. My place is your place for as long as you like.”

Mydei’s chest tightened in a way that wasn’t unpleasant. He opened his mouth to refuse but found himself swallowed by the calm warmth of the space. The farmhouse didn’t demand anything of him. It didn’t judge. It didn’t expect him to perform, to command, to be anyone but himself.

“I… alright,” he finally said, his voice quieter than usual. “Just for a while.”

Phainon’s grin softened, almost shy now, and he stepped aside, gesturing toward the door.

Mydei let himself step forward, his boots scuffing softly against the porch. Inside, the farmhouse smelled of woodsmoke, dried herbs, and something warm that made his chest loosen despite himself. Sunlight pooled on the floor in lazy rectangles. He realized, with a small, unspoken surprise, that his always-tensed shoulders felt lighter.

He glanced at Phainon, who was already bustling around as if it was normal for people to just show up at his home, and couldn’t help a tiny, reluctant smile.

He wasn’t used to this: to the quiet, the comfort…, the feeling that maybe, for a moment, he could just exist. And somehow, Phainon had made it feel effortless.

For the first time since leaving the capital, Mydei didn’t feel like he was running from something.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Pomegranate
chapters.html:
Several days passed before Mydei realized how easily Phainon’s rhythms had begun to seep into him.

Morning came early on the farm but somehow, waking to the soft clatter of Phainon stumbling around the kitchen or cursing at an uncooperative drawer felt… grounding. A strange kind of peace, the sort that didn’t demand anything from him.

He wasn’t sure when it happened, but at some point Phainon had stopped calling him “Mystery Guy” and started calling him “hey, you,” which was somehow worse.

And Mydei helped anyway; not out of obligation nor because he liked farm work, but because Phainon would look over his shoulder with that infuriating bright grin and say, “Thanks,” in a tone so warm it made Mydei’s stomach twist in ways he didn’t care to name.

This morning was no different.

Mydei stood beside him in the orchard, the rising sun painting the fields in a soft, amber glow. Phainon was crouched near one of the pomegranate trees, hands on his knees, brow furrowed in concentration.

“It’s not just the pomegranates,” Phainon muttered, prodding the base of the trunk. “The olives look off too. And don’t get me started on the wheat.”

Mydei crouched beside him, inspecting the roots. “Rot?”

“Maybe. But it shouldn’t spread this fast.” Phainon glanced up, squinting at him. “You think it’s just bad luck?”

“No,” Mydei said immediately.

Phainon huffed. “Optimistic as always.”

“You don’t want optimism,” Mydei said, brushing soil aside. “You want the truth.”

“And what’s the truth?”

Something had been gnawing at the edges of the crops. Small, oddly shaped marks.

“Something’s been here,” he said, rising to his feet. “Something unnatural.”

Phainon stood too, dusting off his hands. “Like what?”

Mydei stared out over the quiet fields. The morning breeze ruffled the wheat in uneven shivers, patches missing.

“Like something that doesn’t want you harvesting at all.”

Phainon let out a low whistle. “Great. Just my luck, huh?”

Mydei glanced at him. “You scared?”

“Of course I’m scared,” Phainon said brightly, hands on hips. “But I bet that body of yours is enough to defend both of us.”

Mydei’s lips twitched. “HKS.”

“I don’t know what that means but from the past few days I can feel it’s not something kind.”

They went back to work —inspecting the fields, checking the irrigation, arguing over which tools were better. Phainon accused Mydei of overthinking. Mydei accused Phainon of not thinking at all.

When noon came, the heat pressed down on them. Phainon wiped his forehead dramatically, tossing himself into the shade beneath a small pomegranate tree.

“Break time,” he announced.

“You just sat down,” Mydei said.

Phainon patted the ground beside him. “Exactly. Come here. I’m dying.”

“You’re not dying.”

“I could be dying.”

Mydei gave him a long, unimpressed stare. Phainon widened his eyes even more, sticking his lower lip out in exaggerated suffering.

Mydei sighed loudly and sat.

“Thank the titans,” Phainon murmured, leaning back on his elbows.

Mydei didn’t look directly at him, but he could feel the heat of Phainon’s bare forearms beside him, the faint rise and fall of his chest, the scent of sun-warmed skin and crushed leaves.

They were too close.

Phainon nudged him with his knee. “Hey.”

“What.”

“You’ve been quieter today.”

“I’m always quiet.”

“Not with me.”

Mydei’s breath caught, but Phainon didn’t seem to notice the effect his words had.

Phainon leaned a little closer, studying him with that gentle, irritatingly perceptive look he kept using on Mydei, like he could see straight through the armor Mydei had spent years wearing.

“Are you worried? About the fields?”

“About whatever’s in them,” Mydei corrected.

Phainon hummed thoughtfully. “Well… I’m glad you’re here.”

Mydei’s chest tightened. He didn’t want that to matter, but it mattered anyway.

“Someone’s gotta keep me from getting eaten.”

“…I’m not staying because of that.”

“I know.” Phainon leaned closer, voice dropping to something lower, softer. “But I like that you are.”

Mydei’s pulse stuttered.

The breeze shifted, carrying the scent of sun and pomegranates, brushing loose strands of Phainon’s hair across his forehead. Mydei’s fingers twitched —heat pooling low in his stomach in a way he absolutely refused to acknowledge.

Phainon noticed the tension, his grin turning slow, teasing, almost wicked. “What? Can’t handle a compliment?”

Mydei glared. “Stop talking.”

Phainon’s smile widened. “Make me.”

The way he said it, warm and challenging and far too inviting, made Mydei feel something coil tight inside him.

He looked away, jaw clenching.

“Phainon,” he warned, but it sounded nothing like a warning.

Phainon tilted his head, eyes flickering down to Mydei’s mouth for half a second. His voice dropped to a low hum. “Yes?”

Phainon leaned in and Mydei’s breath stilled. However, Phainon stopped for a mere moment as if giving Mydei every chance to pull back.

Mydei didn’t.

Their legs brushed. Their shoulders pressed together. The world narrowed to the warm space between their mouths.

Phainon’s eyes flicked to his lips once again.

“I wish I knew your name so I could call you, too,” he whispered, soft enough that it was barely a breath, but a plea.

Mydei swallowed hard, pulse hammering. He hated how much he wanted to tell Phainon the truth and see for himself how much his title could change someone’s opinion of him.

Mydeimos, Prince of Castrum Kremnos.
The man Phainon shouldn’t be leaning toward under a pomegranate tree.

He could feel it rising in his throat before he could stop it.

“Phainon,” he murmured, voice shaking, “I’m…”

It hung there, suspended between them.

His lips parted.

He was going to say it.

He wanted to say it.

“My-”

A violent rustle tore through the wheat. Both of them jerked and then, the moment broke apart like glass.

Phainon sat up. “Did you hear—?”

The sound came again. Low, skittering, too fast.

Mydei was on his feet instantly, spear in hand before he even realized he’d moved.

Something was out there.

Watching. Circling. Waiting.

Phainon didn’t freeze, nor did he gasp or ask what to do, as if this was a daily thing for him. He shot to his feet with a sharp inhale and sprinted.

“Phainon—!”

Phainon darted across the orchard with surprising speed, vanishing inside the farmhouse. Mydei cursed under his breath. A heartbeat later, the door slammed open again and he emerged, sword in hand.

Phainon jogged back toward him, breath quick but eyes sharp. “Alright. I’m ready.”

Mydei blinked at him. “You… own a sword.”

For someone who insisted Mydei would be the one doing all the fighting, Phainon held that sword like he’d been born with it in hand.

Phainon rolled his eyes. “I live near woods and fields. What did you expect me to fight monsters with? Harsh language?”

“That, or nets.”

“That was one time,” Phainon hissed.

He came to stand beside Mydei, and for a moment the heat from earlier, the tension… it all simmered, hot and confusing, under the surface.

But then the wheat shook again, violently.

Mydei’s muscles coiled tight. “Stay behind me.”

Phainon didn’t hesitate. He stepped in front of him.

“No.” His voice was quiet but firm. “Not happening.”

Mydei grabbed his wrist. “Phainon—”

“What would the village think of me if I let my guest get hurt in my own farm?,” Phainon said, eyes locked on the trembling wheat. “Don’t worry, I’m used to this.”

Mydei felt something hot and furious rise in his throat. “Phainon, I swear—”

But the wheat rippled and both of them turned toward it. Shoulder to shoulder now, weapons raised.

Phainon exhaled once, steadying himself. “Okay. On three...”

Mydei muttered, “If you count wrong…”

“One…” Phainon ignored him. “Two…”

“Phainon, don’t.”

“THREE!”

The wheat exploded outward. A blur of claws and teeth and mottled hide sprang at them with a shriek.

Mydei lunged, but Phainon did too.

He wasn’t reckless this time —he moved with purpose. Quick, decisive, practiced.

Their bodies brushed as they stepped into the creature’s path.

Mydei’s spear thrust forward; Phainon’s blade arced downward.

A perfectly timed strike, accidental synchronicity. Like they’d trained together for years instead of days.

The creature screeched and veered back into the wheat, injured but not down. The entire field rustled now, and there were even more of them.

Phainon sucked in a breath. “That 's…”

“A pack,” Mydei finished grimly.

Phainon tightened his grip on the sword.

Despite the fear curling in his gut, Mydei felt a fierce warmth spread through his chest.

Because Phainon stood beside him and not behind him.
Because Phainon had run for his sword like it was second nature, just like he had gone for his spear like it was second nature for him too.

He felt like Phainon and him were too alike for their own good, and that almost made Mydei smile in such a moment.

Mydei shifted closer, their arms brushing. “Stay with me.”

Phainon gave a small, breathless laugh. “Of course. You are not getting rid of me so easily.”

The wheat hissed, the monsters moved. And together they braced for the next attack.

By the time the last creature fell, Mydei’s arms ached, his lungs burned, and the metallic taste of adrenaline sat thick at the back of his tongue. The wheatfield was torn in uneven patches, trampled stalks and streaks of blood marking where the pack had circled them.

Phainon lowered his sword only once the hissing in the wheat faded to silence.

For a long moment, neither of them spoke.

Then Phainon drew in a shaky breath and let out a humorless laugh. “Well, that’s one way to ruin a perfectly good lunch break.”

Mydei huffed, the closest he came to laughing. “You call that good?”

“You were there,” Phainon shot back, pointing the tip of his sword vaguely in Mydei’s direction. “You’re lucky you’re pretty when you’re annoyed, or else I would’ve complained more.”

Mydei blinked at him. “…What.”

“What?” Phainon repeated innocently, even as his chest heaved.

“You—” Mydei gestured at him with his spear. “You’re bleeding.”

Phainon looked down at the thin cut across his arm. “Huh… So I am.”

And then he swayed.

Mydei dropped his spear so fast it hit the ground with a soft thud. “Sit down. Now.”

“Bossy,” Phainon muttered, but he obeyed, plopping onto the ground with a wince. “You’d make a terrible farmer. Farmers don’t get to command people.”

Mydei knelt beside him, checking the wound. “If you died, who would finish the harvest?”

“Oho,” Phainon grinned weakly. “So that’s why you care.”

Mydei ignored him, because the alternative was acknowledging the way his heart had lurched when Phainon stumbled.

He unfastened the clasp of his right gauntlet, sliding it off with a metallic scrape. Beneath it, a strip of soft linen was wrapped around his forearm for padding. He tore it free in one decisive motion.

“Hold still,” he muttered.

Mydei wound the linen around Phainon’s arm, firm but careful, fingers brushing warm skin.

Phainon watched him the entire time. Too closely. Too softly.

“Thank you,” he said when Mydei finished —and the sincerity in it hit Mydei harder than any creature in that field.

“…Let’s go inside,” Mydei muttered. “Before something else crawls out of the ground.”

Phainon stood, brushing wheat from his hair. “You coming with me? To protect me?”

“No,” Mydei said flatly. “To make sure you don’t trip over your own feet.”

Phainon laughed, the sound bright and utterly unbothered by how close they’d come to serious danger. He bumped his shoulder into Mydei’s as he walked past. “Same thing.”

Inside, the air still smelled of herbs and something lightly sweet —the remnants of whatever Phainon had been baking that morning.

Phainon collapsed onto a stool, sword tossed haphazardly onto the table.

“You should clean that,” Mydei said.

Phainon raised an eyebrow. “Worried about my sword?”

“I’m worried you’ll cut your hand open trying to handle it like an idiot.”

Phainon beamed. “You are worried.”

Mydei rubbed the bridge of his nose. “You’re impossible.”

“And you like me anyway.”

Mydei did not answer, which Phainon took as another victory.

Mydei busied himself instead, grabbing a bowl of water and cloth, carefully wiping the blood and dirt from Phainon’s arm. He tried to focus on the task —not how quiet Phainon had gone and definitely not the warmth of Phainon’s skin.

“Hey,” Phainon said softly.

Mydei didn’t look up. “What.”

“Back there… you were about to tell me your name.”

Mydei froze mid-wipe.

Phainon leaned forward slightly, eyes searching his face with a gentle curiosity that made Mydei's stomach tighten. “You were. Don’t deny it. You said ‘My…’ with that weird little dramatic pause, like you were about to reveal something scandalous.”

“It wasn’t dramatic,” Mydei snapped too quickly.

“It kind of was,” Phainon said with a small grin.

Mydei swallowed. Hard.

The truth teetered on the edge of his tongue again, but Phainon kept talking, filling the silence before Mydei could fall into it.

“You don’t have to tell me,” he said, tone softening. “Not until you want to. I’ll keep calling you Mystery Guy. Or hey-you. Or Wheat Slayer. Ooh, or Shoulder-Puncher—”

Mydei groaned. “Please stop speaking.”

“Fine,” Phainon relented. “But you will tell me one day.”

Mydei didn’t respond, but his chest tightened in a way that wasn’t unpleasant.

“Here,” Phainon said, sliding something toward him on the table.

Mydei frowned. “What is that?”

“A pomegranate.”

“Why.”

“Because you look like you’re about to fight me again and I’d rather you chew something instead.”

Mydei stared at him.

Phainon stared back, smile warm and lopsided, hair sticking up, cheeks flushed from battle and sun.

Something in Mydei cracked, something quiet and uncontrollable.

“You’re ridiculous,” Mydei murmured.

“I know.” Phainon grinned wider. “But you’re still here, so who is the more ridiculous one?”

HKS. Mydei didn’t have an answer for that.

So he sat. And stayed.

Close enough that their shoulders brushed.

Close enough that Phainon’s knee nudged his again, deliberately this time.

Mydei’s breath caught, but he didn’t move. He didn’t dare.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Prophecy
chapters.html:
Sunlight spilled through the windows, painting the floor in soft amber streaks. The previous day’s battle had left the wheat fields torn and quiet, but inside the farmhouse, the air hummed with a different tension.

Phainon sat cross-legged on the floor, sword leaning against the table, eyes tracing the marks left by the creatures on the walls. His brow was furrowed, hands restless.

“So,” he said, finally breaking the silence, “we need to figure out what those things were. And why were they so fixated on the crops.”

Mydei leaned against the counter, arms crossed, watching him with calm detachment. “Focused on the fields?”

“Yes. The wheat, the olives, the pomegranates…” Phainon’s fingers tapped the floor nervously. “It’s like they weren’t after us, really. They were after the harvests themselves.”

“Monsters that care about food?” Mydei’s voice was flat, though his chest tightened anyway. The monsters did go after the harvest and Phainon. Just not him.

“Not ordinary monsters,” Phainon said, tone dropping, low and serious. “There’s… an old prophecy. About the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.”

Mydei froze slightly.

Phainon leaned back on his hands, frowning. “It says the prince will face a scourge that feeds on the land. That the land and its people suffer wherever he goes. That’s all I know. I’ve only heard of it from the older villagers but…, ” he hesitated. “These creatures, they might be tied to it.”

Mydei’s hands clenched at his sides. Every instinct screamed: flee and hide. Yet another part —the part that remembered the villages, the farmers and the fields— whispered that running meant letting everyone down.

Phainon’s voice softened, drawing him back from spiraling thoughts. “I don’t know how to stop it. But if the prophecy is true, and if the prince is out there somewhere…” He paused, eyes scanning Mydei’s face with careful curiosity. “Well, I guess he will have to face it.”

Mydei swallowed hard, the weight pressing on him. He didn’t tell Phainon he was the prince. Not yet… not until he decided what to do.

Phainon sighed and pushed to his feet. “Alright, enough brooding. The orchard can wait. We need new supplies: grain, olives, maybe some new seedlings. We should head to the city. And, you know, maybe avoid getting eaten while we’re at it.”

“You just like making me worry,” Mydei muttered, grabbing his spear.

“And you like pretending you don’t care,” Phainon shot back, grinning.

Mydei rolled his eyes, but a corner of his mouth twitched upward despite himself.

The road to Aedes Elysiae’s main port was quiet, dust curling under their boots with every step. The sun was high now, warm on their shoulders, but neither spoke much. Phainon seemed to hum to himself, tapping the hilt of his sword occasionally, while Mydei kept his spear loosely in hand, eyes scanning the horizon more out of habit than fear.

Finally, Phainon broke the silence. “You know, you really don’t have to scowl the whole time we walk. It’s exhausting for me.”

“My face isn’t a weapon,” Mydei muttered, not looking at him.

Phainon grinned. “No, but it’s dangerously close.”

Mydei groaned. Phainon had that effect on him.

By the time they reached their destination, the sun had softened into late morning. The marketplace was bustling with farmers, merchants, and children darting between stalls. The air smelled of baked bread and fresh flowers.

“Alright,” Phainon said, scanning the stalls. “Grain first, then something edible that isn’t cursed by some unknown monster.”

“Noted,” Mydei replied, voice flat, though he allowed himself a small smirk when Phainon mimed dramatic horror at the thought of bad produce.

They weaved through the crowd, bickering over the best prices, arguing over which sacks of grain looked sturdier, and teasing each other over who carried more weight. For a moment, the weight of the prophecy, the creatures, and the torn fields felt distant, replaced by this mundane but comforting rhythm.

Then Mydei’s gaze caught something pinned to a wooden post at the edge of the square.

“The crown prince of Castrum Kremnos is dead,” it proclaimed in bold, official letters.

Mydei froze mid-step. His pulse stuttered. The words were simple, yet the authority behind them made his stomach twist. He was alive. He had always been alive. And yet here it was: proof that everyone thought otherwise.

Disbelief curled tight in his chest. How could they say that? How could they lie like this? His thoughts tangled, and a flicker of something darker coiled beneath the disbelief: betrayal.

Did my father send me away knowing this would happen? Mydei’s jaw clenched as his fists tightened around his spear.

Phainon noticed his pause. “What?”

“…Nothing,” Mydei said quickly, shaking his head, forcing himself to appear disinterested.

Phainon frowned, eyes narrowing. “That ‘nothing’ looks like someone just saw a ghost.”

“Just… village news,” Mydei muttered, forcing his legs to move again, but his gaze kept flicking back to the poster, a thread pulling his thoughts down a spiraling path.

Phainon followed his eyes and whistled softly. “Oof. That’s harsh. But… the prince? How could that be? Isn’t he well known for being a blood-driven guy?”

Mydei’s chest tightened. “Whether it’s fake or not… people will believe it.”

Phainon stepped closer, lowering his voice. “Belief doesn’t make it true.”

Mydei swallowed hard, feeling the weight of the prophecy press down like an iron chain. 

The scourge. The sacrifice. The crown prince.

Each word seemed to echo in his mind. Now all the events that had been happening all clicked together, a pattern he hadn’t wanted to see. Was this all part of their plan? Was my exile meant to protect them, or to ensure they would think I was dead so they wouldn’t go for my head?

“Let’s just get the supplies,” he muttered finally, forcing his voice back to normal, though every step felt heavier, burdened with questions he wasn’t ready to voice.

Phainon gave him a sidelong glance, sharp and perceptive, like he could read every hesitation. “Right, the supplies.”

They moved through the market, bickering softly over grain quality, their usual rhythm a fragile shield against the unease that had settled over him. The poster still lingered in the back of his mind, a reminder that the truth and the lies could reshape everything.

Mydei’s hands ached from gripping his spear too tightly, but he couldn’t let go. Every face in the crowd felt like a reminder of what he had been erased from. He had been alive all this time, hidden in plain sight, yet the world had moved on as if he were nothing more than a story in a dusty tome.

The poster burned in his mind. The crown prince is dead. The words weren’t just ink on paper —they were a verdict, a lie woven into law and custom, and yet here he was, breathing.

The betrayal twisted deep, sharper than any blade he had ever faced. His father, the council, the carefully crafted exile… all of it flashed through his thoughts. Did they think keeping him hidden would save the kingdom, or were they willing to sacrifice him in the shadows for some abstract “greater good”?

His pulse pounded. The prophecy wasn’t just words; it was a trap, a chain that tethered him to the land, to the suffering he had witnessed, and to a death that everyone believed had already claimed him.

What do I do now? His mind raced. Fight the scourge himself? Return to Castrum Kremnos and reclaim what was rightfully his, or stay hidden and hope the prophecy doesn't catch up to him?

And then there was Phainon. Warm, oblivious to the gravity of the world pressing down on Mydei, but steadfast, ready to face danger without hesitation. The thought of dragging him into the chaos —or worse, losing him because of it— made Mydei’s stomach twist. He couldn’t allow anyone to die on his account.

He exhaled slowly, grounding himself. The first step was simple: gather the supplies, return to the farmhouse, fortify, plan.

But he also knew one thing: he couldn’t pretend to be an ordinary guest any longer. Not if the prophecy was real, if the shadows were following him.

He would move carefully, quietly, like he had all these years, but he wouldn’t hide forever. And maybe, just maybe, he’d let Phainon in on the truth when the time was right. Or maybe he wouldn’t.

Either way, Mydei had a plan forming, cold and precise beneath the ache of betrayal. Survive. Protect. And, if fate demanded it, fight.

For now, though, he forced his shoulders to relax, muttering under his breath: “One thing at a time.”

Phainon, catching the mutter, grinned. “See? You can sound normal. Small victories, Mystery Guy.”

Mydei shot him a sharp look, but couldn’t stop the faint twitch of amusement at the corner of his lips. For a brief moment, the weight of crowns, prophecies, and lies eased just enough for a shard of something almost like peace.

Almost.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Hesitation
chapters.html:
Mydei and Phainon returned with sacks of provisions, their shoulders slightly sunburned and their shoes dust-dappled from the walk.

Phainon dropped his haul on the table with a flourish. “Mission accomplished. The market hasn’t beaten us yet!”

Mydei raised an eyebrow. “Mission accomplished? You only saved yourself from a bad deal with the grain merchant.”

“What about you?” Phainon countered, tugging a rogue stalk of wheat from Mydei’s shoulder. “Did you negotiate with your charm, or did you threaten with that scary glare of yours?”

“My glare works just fine, thank you,” Mydei muttered, brushing off the wheat. 

Phainon leaned against the counter grinning, eyes flicking toward Mydei. “You know, for someone who’s supposed to be the silent and calm type… you’re awfully twitchy when I poke fun at you.”

“I am not,” Mydei said sharply, then caught himself. He couldn’t deny the quickening of his pulse when Phainon’s hand brushed his as they both reached for the same bag of figs.

“Uh-huh,” Phainon said, smirking. “Not twitchy at all.”

Mydei shot him a look that could have melted steel. “Maybe you just like making me react.”

Phainon’s grin softened. He stepped closer than necessary, tilting his head. “Maybe I do. I like seeing that fire behind your calm exterior.”

Mydei’s chest tightened. He had spent years practicing restraint, hiding his true personality, and yet there was Phainon: unflinching, persistent, somehow warm in the middle of all the chaos.

Mydei blinked and looked away, shoving the next sack onto the table.

Phainon crouched slightly to adjust something on the lower shelf, brushing their shoulders together. His voice was soft, teasing, but with an undertone that made Mydei’s stomach twist. “Careful,” he said. “You’re not making it easy for me to stay out of your way.”

Mydei felt the heat rise. “I’m not trying to—” His words faltered, caught between the truth he couldn’t tell and the pull he didn’t want to resist.

Phainon straightened, a slow grin spreading across his handsome face, and leaned just a fraction closer, close enough that Mydei could feel his warmth.

“You’re tense,” he said lightly. “Relax a little. Or are you keeping it all to lash at me later?”

Mydei’s fingers flexed around the edge of the table, grounding himself.

He wanted to push back, to tease, to distract himself from the guilt curling tight in his chest. The truth about who he was, what he carried, the prophecy; it was a barrier he couldn’t cross yet. And Phainon didn’t deserve the weight of it.

“I’m fine,” he finally managed, voice low. “Just… thinking.”

Phainon’s grin softened, but his eyes didn’t waver. “Right,” he echoed, voice smooth but teasing. “I’ll let you stew a little longer, then.”

Mydei swallowed hard. Every instinct screamed at him to flee. He didn’t push Phainon away, but he didn’t let the space shrink, either. The tension between them stretched taut, delicate and dangerous.

Outside, the wind rustled the trees, whispering reminders of the fields lost and the creatures that still prowled. Inside, the farmhouse felt impossibly small, crowded with unspoken words and almost-touching closeness.

For the first time in days, Mydei let himself feel something besides uneasiness —something that he couldn’t name yet.

He didn’t know how much time they had before the prophecy’s shadow grew longer, but for now, he let himself linger in the small moments.

The farmhouse was quiet except for the soft rustle of sacks and the occasional clink of jars. Mydei was stacking provisions on the shelves, methodical and precise, when Phainon moved behind him.

He reached for a jar of honey, brushing dust off the top with a finger. His hand lingered a moment longer than necessary near Mydei’s. “You always stack them so neatly,” he said softly. “You know, if I didn’t need to stay alert, I would just watch you do this all day.”

Mydei stiffened, trying not to notice how close Phainon was standing. “I’m efficient,” he muttered, though his pulse betrayed him.

As Phainon straightened, he nudged a nearby sack to balance it, and their shoulders brushed. Mydei froze, a jolt of awareness shooting through him as the brush lingered just a heartbeat too long. He gripped the edge of the shelf, heart hammering.

“You really do overthink everything,” Phainon said softly, almost a whisper. “Even this.”

“I have to,” Mydei replied, voice tight. “Someone has to keep track of everything.”

Phainon tilted his head, studying him with a teasing spark in his eyes. “Everything, huh? That includes me, then?”

The question hung in the air longer than it should have. Mydei’s heart thudded painfully in his chest. He knew Phainon wasn’t asking just about chores.

He shifted, trying to create space, but the small room worked against him.

A sudden stumble sent the sack of beans tipping toward the floor. Without thinking, Phainon lunged forward, catching it and Mydei at the same time. Their faces were impossibly close, breath mingling. Mydei froze, panic and something else rising in his chest.

“We’re supposed to survive this together, remember? Not… topple over into each other,” Phainon whispered, his forehead nearly brushing Mydei’s.

“I…” Mydei choked, looking anywhere but at him. “I’m fine.”

“Sure you are,” Phainon said, a smirk tugging at the corner of his mouth. 

Their hands both lingered on the sack for a heartbeat too long. Then, with a clumsy shuffle, Phainon straightened, stepping back, but the tension didn’t go with him. Mydei’s pulse was still hammering, the heat in his cheeks refusing to fade.

Phainon’s grin softened, eyes warmer now. “You know… if we keep brushing shoulders like this, I might start to think it’s intentional.”

“Don’t be ridiculous,” Mydei muttered, but even as he said it, his fingers flexed around the edge of the shelf, a little too tightly.

For a moment, the world outside felt distant. The farmhouse seemed cramped for two big men, but it was theirs, for now. However, it was impossible to ignore the closeness and those accidental brushes between them. 

Phainon’s voice broke the silence again, softer this time, almost tender. “You’re hiding something from me, Mystery Guy. I don’t know what it is, but I’ll wait.”

Mydei’s jaw tightened. He couldn’t tell him yet. Not until he understood everything his curse entailed. And in spite of that, he couldn’t bring himself to push Phainon away, not entirely.

Phainon stepped closer, his fingers brushing against the small braid at the nape of Mydei’s neck, twirling it gently between his fingers. “You know,” he murmured, voice low and teasing, “when we stand this close, I end up forgetting what we were supposed to be doing.”

Mydei’s pulse spiked. He wanted to step back, to regain the distance he knew they should have, but his body betrayed him, rooted in place by the warmth and quiet confidence radiating from Phainon.

“HKS. You’re too close,” Mydei muttered, voice tight, though it lacked conviction.

“Am I?” Phainon asked softly, tilting his head, eyes searching his face. “Or are you just not saying no?”

Mydei swallowed, chest tight. He could feel Phainon’s breath near his ear, and the teasing lilt in his voice made something coil painfully in his stomach. Every instinct screamed at him and yet he didn’t move.

Phainon’s hand lingered on the braid, brushing a strand of hair loose, fingers ghosting over the nape of his neck. “I think…,” he started, voice dropping a notch, “I could get used to this.”

Those words made Mydei’s chest tighten even more. His hands flexed at his sides, gripping the shelf to anchor himself. He wanted to shove Phainon back, but his body betrayed him again, a shiver running down his spine.

Before he could think, Phainon leaned forward slightly, and in an almost unconscious movement, their lips brushed. Mydei’s eyes widened, heart hammering, heat flooding his cheeks.

The kiss lingered in his senses longer than it lasted, a spark that left him reeling. Guilt clawed at him immediately —he couldn’t let this happen, not with all the secrets he carried. He shoved himself back a fraction, shaking his head. “Phainon, I…”

Phainon froze, surprised, a shadow of concern passing over his features. “Hey… what’s wrong?”

“I can’t—” Mydei choked out, voice tight. “There’s… too much you don’t know.”

Phainon’s teasing smirk faltered, replaced with patient understanding. “Then I’ll wait for you to trust me,” he said, letting his hand drop gently.

Mydei swallowed hard and straightened himself, wanting to focus on the sacks and jars in front of him.

Phainon, sensing the shift, let out a quiet, almost indulgent sigh. “You really are impossible, you know that?” he said, voice threaded with something tender.

“I—” Mydei began, then stopped, frustration and guilt knotting in his chest. He wanted to speak, to explain himself… and yet, he couldn’t. Not fully. “I’m sorry.”

Phainon stepped back a little, enough to give Mydei space but not enough to erase the tension lingering between them. “Don’t be,” he said simply. 

A fragile quiet settled over the room. The wind rattled the farmhouse shutters, a reminder of the world outside, of all the danger still waiting for them. But inside, amidst the jars, sacks, and dust motes dancing in the fading sunlight, there was a brief moment of calm —a small pocket of normalcy, of closeness.

Mydei exhaled slowly, trying to steady his racing heart. “We should finish here,” he said, voice tight but firm. “Then we need to check the fields. We can’t let our guard down.”

Phainon’s grin returned, softer this time. “Right. Fields first. Heart-melting brooding later,” he said, a playful glint in his eye.

“…Don’t make me regret doing chores with you,” Mydei muttered, shoulders stiff, but the smallest edge of a smile tugged at his lips.

Phainon chuckled, a sound low and teasing, brushing a stray lock of hair from Mydei’s forehead before stepping toward the door. “Oh, I’m counting on it.”

As they moved to leave the farmhouse, side by side but not touching, the air between them hummed with all the unspoken words. For now, they had each other in this fragile, fleeting moment and that, Mydei thought, was enough.

The door closed behind them with a soft click, leaving the house empty, yet holding the fragile seed of new beginnings.

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

TW: NSFW!

The afternoon sun pressed down and the air inside had the weight of unspoken words. Neither could shake the lingering tension from the other day.

Phainon leaned casually against the counter, watching Mydei reorganize a crooked stack with the same irritated precision he used on everything. “I bet you’re going to rearrange them again after dinner,” he said, voice annoyingly certain.

“No, I’m not,” Mydei muttered, even though he absolutely was.

“You are,” Phainon said, reaching over to fix a sack Mydei hadn’t gotten to yet. Except he nudged it too far, and it slid forward, teetering.

Mydei lunged to catch it, bumping into Phainon with a sharp exhale. “Can you not make things worse?”

“You’re welcome,” Phainon replied, as if he’d intended the chaos. “I just saved you from having to reorganize the whole thing.”

“You caused the problem,” Mydei snapped.

Phainon grinned. “Only because I know how much you love fixing my mistakes.”

Mydei glared, grabbing the sack firmly, pushing it back into place. “If you touched things properly, maybe—”

“Properly?” Phainon scoffed. He nudged another sack with the tip of his boot, the barest push, just enough to make it tilt dangerously. “Like this?”

Mydei’s jaw dropped. “Don’t.”

The sack listed.

Mydei caught it at the last second, nearly losing his balance.

Phainon laughed. “See? You’re quick. Very impressive.”

“Stop doing that,” Mydei growled.

“Why?” Phainon tilted his head. “Afraid you’ll lose your rhythm?”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed. “Afraid you’ll mess up everything in under a minute.”

Phainon straightened. “Oh? So you think you’d do better?”

Mydei crossed his arms. “I know I would.”

Phainon’s smile sharpened. “Then show me.”

Mydei blinked. “Show you what?”

“Which one of us can stack these faster.” He nudged a different sack with his foot. This time wasn’t enough to topple it, but enough to make Mydei bristle. “You said you are better than me, right? Prove it.”

Mydei set the sack down with controlled fury. “I didn’t say that.”

“You implied it,” Phainon said, already rolling up his sleeves. “And I’m choosing to take it personally.”

Mydei exhaled a long-suffering sigh. “You’re impossible.”

“And you’re stalling,” Phainon said, stepping too close for comfort. “Unless you don’t want to see the reality?”

Mydei felt his pulse spike at the proximity. “Fine. But when you embarrass yourself, that’s on you.”

Phainon grinned. “Loser does anything the winner asks?”

Mydei’s grin went feral. “Deal.”

By the time the challenge was over, the farmhouse looked like two storms had collided and shaken hands out of mutual respect.

Mydei stood with his arms crossed and breath uneven. His cheeks were flushed from exertion and definitely not from Phainon’s constant commentary.

Phainon rested his hands on his hips, equally breathless. “Well,” he huffed, “I think it’s obvious who won.”

“Yes,” Mydei said dryly, “me.”

Phainon barked a laugh. “You? Did you see your side? One sack was literally upside down.”

“It was structurally stable.”

“It was wrong.”

Mydei’s glare sharpened. “And you put one of yours on top of a jar of pickles.”

“It fit!”

They both stared at each other.

Then, unfortunately for both their pride, they turned to the shelves at the same time. It was undeniably…

“…a draw,” they said in unison, the words tasting like ash.

Mydei sighed. “I hate this.”

“Me too.”

They stood there in a silence vibrating with the weight of their stupid bet.

Finally, Phainon puffed out a breath. “Well, a deal’s a deal. Winner gets anything they want, so I guess we both get the prize.”

Mydei went still. “That's not—”

“It is now,” Phainon cut in, stepping so close that Mydei could feel the heat rolling off him. “Unless you’re scared?”

Mydei bared his teeth. “Never.”

“Good.” Phainon stepped closer, leaning just enough to be inconvenient. “Then I'll cash in first.”

Mydei swallowed. “What do you want?”

Phainon’s grin softened into something slow and warm. “Simple. You’re coming with me to wash off all this dust. There’s a bathing spring not too far from the orchard. Perfect for…”
His eyes flicked down Mydei’s form and back up.
“…relaxing.”

Mydei’s pulse stuttered. “You want me to bathe with you?”

“Well, someone needs to make sure you don’t drown yourself to death in the water.”

“That’s—”

“And,” Phainon added, stepping even closer, “I don’t take a no for an answer. I intend to enjoy my reward.”

Mydei opened his mouth, closed it, then muttered, “Fine. But only because you clearly need supervision.”

“Mm.” Phainon smirked. “Whatever helps you sleep at night.”

Mydei turned away, pretending not to burn.

But just as he stepped outside, he said without looking back,

“After the bath…”
His voice lowered a notch.
“...you’re doing what I want.”

Phainon stopped in the doorway, breath catching almost imperceptibly. “Yeah? And what’s that?”

Mydei didn’t answer. Didn’t need to, actually.

As he walked ahead, distance growing between them, Phainon let out a soft exhale he hadn't meant to release.

A crooked smile tugged at his lips.

“…I’m the one who has lost already.”

The path behind the orchard had been left to its own devices for years. Tall grass brushed their calves, seed-heads scattering like tiny sparks whenever Mydei’s stride cut too close. Cicadas droned in the heat, a low, pulsing throb that felt almost indecent after the farmhouse’s stubborn silence.

They rounded a final bend where the pomegranate trees gave way to a stand of ancient willows, their drooping branches trailing the ground like curtains. There, tucked into the hillside, the hot spring opened up.

It wasn’t grand —just a natural hollow in the rock, no wider than a small room— but the earth had shaped it perfectly. The pool itself steamed gently, its surface the color of clouded turquoise where minerals had painted the bottom. Tiny ripples kissed the edges and retreated as if the spring was breathing.

Ferns clung to the cracks in the rock, dripping lazily. Overhead, the willows filtered the light into green-gold shards that danced across the steam, turning the air itself hazy and half-lit.

It felt secret, like they were trespassing.

Mydei stopped at the edge, boots scuffing against warm stone. Behind him, Phainon let out a low, appreciative hum that vibrated straight through Mydei’s spine.

“Told you,” Phainon murmured, voice roughened by heat and something else. “It’s perfect.”

Mydei’s stomach tightened. “It’s a bath, Phainon. Not a divine revelation.”

“Depends who you’re bathing with,” Phainon shot back over his shoulder.

Mydei didn’t answer. He was too busy pretending his pulse wasn’t already matching the slow, steady breath of the spring.

Phainon toed off his boots, then peeled his dust-covered shirt over his head with casual confidence. Mydei looked away.

“Any problem?” Phainon asked, amused.

“No,” Mydei said sharply. “Just hurry up.”

Phainon chuckled, stepping into the water with a hiss of satisfaction. “Titans, that feels good… You coming?”

When Phainon finally came, it was with Mydei’s real name torn from his throat like a vow, hips stuttering, spilling deep inside him as he whispered one last time against sweat-slick skin:

“Mydei, my love.”

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

TW: BLOOD AND DEAD PEOPLE !!

Mydei woke to the faint, acrid tang of smoke drifting on the morning air, mingling with the deeper ache that throbbed through his body; a reminder of surrender, of hands and mouths and the weight of secrets finally spilled.

For a disoriented heartbeat, he was back in the palace, the day his father had summoned him to the throne room, the air thick with unspoken judgments, servants' whispers slithering through the corridors like shadows. His chest tightened, breath catching sharp in his throat.

But then the low, wooden beams of the farmhouse ceiling swam into focus above him, the rough weave of the sheets clean against his skin. Someone had washed him while he slept, gentle cloths tracing paths over sweat-slicked limbs, reverent fingers combing through his tangled hair. The tenderness of it stung, a quiet care he hadn't earned.

The other side of the bed was empty, the indent in the mattress already cooling, and panic surged through him like ice water, freezing his veins. Phainon was gone… Of course he was. 

Mydei had let the name slip in the heat of the night, had bared the cursed truth amid gasps and moans, and Phainon —kind, selfless Phainon— must had waited until exhaustion claimed him to slip away into the dawn.

Who wouldn't flee from the prince of ruins, the one whose very existence drew shadows and death like moths to a flame?

Mydei's hands fisted in the sheets, his naked body trembling as he swung his legs over the edge of the bed, ready to bolt before the prophecy could claim another soul.

Then, the door creaked open then, a soft groan of hinges that shattered the silence.

Phainon stepped inside, balancing a wooden tray laden with simple fare: a loaf of burnt bread, a wedge of soft cheese flecked with herbs and a clay mug of creamy milk swirled with tart pomegranate juice that sloshed gently with his steps.

His silver hair was sleep-tousled, catching the faint light filtering through the shutters, and his shirt hung half-buttoned, revealing the broad expanse of his chest marked with faint bruises, badges of their frenzy.

He paused in the doorway, blue eyes softening as they met Mydei's wide, startled gaze.

"You're awake," Phainon said, his voice low and warm, like the rumble of distant thunder that promised rain instead of storm. "I thought you'd sleep till noon after... well, after last night." A crooked grin tugged at his lips, fond and teasing, as he crossed the room and set the tray on the bedside table with a soft clunk.

Mydei stared, the panic ebbing away in slow waves, leaving behind a raw, humiliating vulnerability. His throat worked, words failing him as relief flooded in, hot and unwelcome. "You... stayed."

Phainon's brows furrowed, a flicker of confusion crossing his face.

He sank to one knee in front of Mydei, his large hands settling warm and steady on Mydei's bare knees, thumbs tracing slow circles over the skin. The touch was grounding, intimate, a silent anchor.

"Where else would I go?" he murmured, searching Mydei's face with those piercing blue eyes. "You think I'd leave you after you finally trusted me? After you let me have all of you like that?"

The reminder hit Mydei like a spark to dry tinder. Memories flashed unbidden: Phainon's mouth on him, hot and unrelenting; the way he'd begged, pride shattered; the deep, claiming thrusts that had wrung his name from Phainon's lips like a vow.

Heat crawled up Mydei's neck, blooming across his cheeks in a flush he couldn't hide. He averted his gaze, golden-red eyes dropping to the floor, but Phainon caught his chin gently, tilting his face back up.

"Look at you, blushing like a maiden on her wedding night," Phainon teased, his voice dropping to that husky timbre that made Mydei's pulse stutter. "You were so fierce last night. And then... titans above, the way you fell apart for me, moaning my name while I—"

He leaned in closer, breath ghosting over Mydei's lips, his thumb brushing the swell of Mydei's lower lip in a way that sent shivers racing down his spine.

"I could do it all over again right now, if you'd let me. Watch you come undone, hear you say my name like it's the only word you know."

Mydei's flush deepened to a burning crimson, his skin prickling under Phainon's gaze. He swatted weakly at Phainon's hand.

"HKS," he muttered, voice rough with embarrassment and a lingering ache of want. "It's too early for your nonsense."

Phainon chuckled, the sound rich and affectionate, but he didn't press further. Instead, he rose and nudged the tray closer. 

"Eat, then. You'll need your strength. We're riding to the city today. We are out of salt and lamp oil, and the miller owes me a favor.” His tone left no room for argument, but there was a quiet plea in his eyes, a desire to keep Mydei close after the vulnerability of the night before. “I want you to come with me."

Mydei wanted to protest, to warn him he should leave alone before the shadows caught up, before the prophecy's claws sank into Phainon too. But the steadiness in those blue eyes, the warmth of that touch undid him completely. 

He nodded, silent, and reached for the burnt bread.

The ride to the city was a slow unraveling of the morning's fragile peace.

They took the winding path through the orchards, the horses' hooves crunching softly over fallen leaves dusted with dew. The air was crisp, carrying the scent of ripening fruit and distant woodsmoke, but an undercurrent of unease hummed beneath it all.

Phainon rode beside him, their knees occasionally brushing, a casual intimacy that made Mydei's heart clench, even after all the events that transcurred the night before.

Every so often, Phainon would glance over, his grin boyish and untroubled, murmuring something mundane about the harvest or the weather, as if the world weren't teetering on the edge of ruin.

"You know," Phainon said at one point, his voice casual but laced with that teasing edge, "last night... when you finally said your name? It felt like everything clicked into place. Mydei." He savored the word, rolling it on his tongue like a secret shared. "Suits you better than any alias. Sharp and beautiful."

Mydei's cheeks heated again, the flush returning unbidden. He kept his eyes on the horizon, gripping the reins tighter. "Don't make a habit of it," he grumbled, but there was no bite to the words, only a quiet thrill at hearing his true name spoken without fear.

Phainon laughed softly. "Too late for that."

The city gates loomed ahead as the sun climbed higher, the walls scarred from old sieges, banners fluttering listlessly in the breeze.

Even from afar, the churn of bodies was visible: refugees spilling in from the north, their wagons laden with meager belongings, faces etched with exhaustion and dread. Rumors of monster sightings had swelled the crowds, whispers of shadows creeping closer, devouring villages whole.

As they passed through the gates, the press of people thickened, voices rising in a cacophony of fear and haggling. The market square was a riot of color and chaos: stalls heaped with wilting produce, merchants shouting over one another, children darting underfoot while elders muttered prayers to forgotten gods.

Phainon dismounted first, tying the horses to a post with practiced ease. He reached up to help Mydei down, hands lingering a moment too long on his waist, a subtle squeeze that sent a spark through Mydei's veins.

"Stay close," Phainon murmured, his breath warm against Mydei's ear. "Crowds like this... anything could happen."

Mydei nodded, swallowing against the knot in his throat. The air felt heavier here, charged with unspoken dread.

They wove through the throng, Phainon's broad frame clearing a path, his hand occasionally brushing Mydei's arm in reassurance.

At the miller's stall, Phainon bartered with easy charm, securing their supplies while Mydei hung back, eyes scanning the faces around them —hollow-eyed refugees sharing tales of horrors in hushed tones, guards patrolling with hands on hilts, the sky above a flat, oppressive gray.

Then, without warning, the sky cracked open.

It started with a low rumble, like thunder rolling in from the west, but no storm followed.

Instead, a shadow unfurled across the square: a nightmare given flesh, wings like torn sails flapping with a leathery snap, its maw gaping wide with rows of jagged teeth that gleamed wetly in the light.

Screams erupted, sharp and piercing, as people scattered like leaves in a gale. The creature dove, claws raking through a stall, splintering wood and sending fruit tumbling in bloody arcs.

Phainon shoved Mydei back against a wall, his body a shield, sword drawn in a flash of steel. "Stay behind me!" he barked, voice cutting through the pandemonium. But Mydei was no fragile thing to be guarded. Warrior's instincts surged through him, hot and unyielding; he drew his own spear in a swift motion, shoving past Phainon with a snarl.

"Like I would let you fight alone!" He lunged at the nearest beast, spear thrusting through the air toward its shadowed flank.

The creature twisted away at the last second, unnaturally agile, its claws raking empty space where Mydei's strike should have landed. He pressed forward, undeterred, spear whipping in precise, deadly patterns honed from years of training in palace courtyards. Yet every thrust met only air, every jab veered off as if the monsters were smoke dissolving around him. Claws whistled past his ear, fangs snapped inches from his throat, yet none connected, repelled by some invisible curse that marked him as untouchable.

More shadows descended, twisted forms slithering from alleys, emerging from the rooftops, a horde of teeth and claws and inky blackness. The square dissolved into bedlam: bodies crumpling under talons, blood slicking the cobblestones, cries blending into a single wail of terror. Phainon charged alongside him now, blade swinging in wide arcs, black ichor splattering his shirt as he felled one snarling abomination after another. But Mydei could see the pattern crystallizing amid the chaos: they weren't here for him. They were here because of him.

The prophecy's venom, seeping into the world through his very presence.

A woman's corpse thudded at his feet, her throat a ragged ruin, eyes frozen in accusation.  Mydei didn't flinch; he'd seen death before, dealt it with his own hands in border skirmishes and training yards. 

But this was different.

Her blood was on him, not from his blade, but from the disaster he carried like a plague. Guilt clawed at his chest, sharper than any talon, making his limbs feel heavy, his resolve brittle.

How many more would fall because he dared to exist? Because he dared to linger here, drawing ruin like a magnet?

"That's him!" a voice shouted from the fray, raw with fury. "The crown prince! Look, the beasts won't touch him!"

Heads turned, fingers jabbed like daggers. The whisper spread, igniting like wildfire through dry grass.

"It's the prophecy!"

"He's the one bringing the disaster!"

"Mydeimos, the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos! He lured them here!"

Mydei suddenly couldn't breathe, the air thick with blood and blame. It weighed on him, fracturing the warrior's armor he'd built so carefully, leaving him raw and exposed. His eyes darted through the swirling madness, seeking Phainon. He found him a few paces away, sword buried in the flank of a writhing shadow, chest heaving, silver hair matted with sweat and grime.

Their gazes locked across the carnage. And there it was —the look Mydei had dreaded in his darkest dreams. Not rage, not terror, but a deep, shattering disappointment, etching lines around Phainon's blue eyes, twisting his mouth into a pained grimace. Betrayal flickered there, raw and unspoken: 

How could you hide this? How could you let me love a lie?

If only…

If only Mydei could truly look into Phainon’s eyes, beyond the veil of his own guilt and fear… Then maybe, he would have seen the truth: the confusion knitting those brows, the worry burning bright in that blue gaze, a lover's desperate concern for his safety amid the unrelenting storm.

Phainon's lips parted, as if to call out, to deny the accusations, to bridge the chasm opening between them. But Mydei couldn't bear to hear it, to see that fondness curdle into rejection.

The guilt was too much, a fragile ache that threatened to shatter him entirely.

He turned and ran.

Through the screaming throng, past the fallen and the dying, past the monsters that parted like smoke around him, refusing to claim their harbinger.

He vaulted onto the nearest horse, fingers numb as they gripped the reins, and kicked it into a frantic gallop.

The city blurred into a streak of stone and shadow, the wind whipping tears from his eyes.

Behind him, Phainon's voice rose once, raw and desperate, cutting through the din: "Mydei!"

But the gale tore the name away, scattering it like ashes, and the prince who should have perished long ago rode alone into the waiting ruin.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Return
chapters.html:
The road to Castrum Kremnos stretched like a scar across the land, winding through fields turned fallow by fear and forests whispering of shadows yet to come.

Mydei had ridden it through the entire night without pause, the horse's flanks lathered in sweat, his own body a hollow vessel of guilt and resolve.

The wind carried echoes of the city's screams, his gaze staring up at him from every puddle, every rut in the path.

He had brought this upon them. 

The prophecy's harbinger, the prince of disaster.

There was only one way to end it.

The capital’s walls rose before him just as the first light of dawn broke, banners limp and gates guarded by men whose faces paled at the sight of him. Whispers rippled through the crowd gathered at the entrance, common folk with pitchforks and fearful eyes. 

"It's the prince," one gasped, incredulity twisting her voice as if he were a ghost risen from the grave.

"He is alive?" Another stepped back, hand flying to his throat, terror etching deep lines in his face.

"He's back... we're doomed!"

And beneath the shock and fear simmered hatred, the glares came sharp as daggers, murmurs turning to snarls.

"It’s all his fault," a man spat, fist clenched. "The beasts follow him like dogs. He'll destroy us all!"

Stones skittered at his feet, not quite thrown but close enough to sting.

Mydei didn't meet their eyes.

He dismounted with deliberate slowness, spear slung across his back, and strode through the gates, the weight of their loathing pressing on him like a shroud. His arrival meant nothing but destruction; he knew it, and so did they.

The palace loomed at the city's heart, its marble halls echoing with the hurried footsteps of servants who scattered like leaves before him. Guards flanked him without a word, their grips tight on halberds, leading him to the throne room where the air hung heavy with incense and unspoken dread.

King Eurypon sat upon the throne with Queen Gorgo at his side, their faces drawn and pale under the weight of crowns.

At the sight of Mydei, Eurypon rose, shock widening his eyes, a flicker of something almost like relief softening the lines of his face. Gorgo gasped, a hand pressing to her lips, her eyes filling with tears that spoke of a mother's buried hope.

"Mydeimos," Eurypon breathed, voice rough with emotion. "We thought... the rumors said you were lost in the wilds."

He stepped forward, as if to embrace him, but halted at the steel in Mydei's gaze. Mydei stood rigid, golden, reddish eyes burning through the haze of exhaustion.

"Why?"

The word cracked like a whip in the silent room.

 "Why didn't you tell me? All these years, you let me believe it was my 'feral' nature, my need to 'connect with the people.' But it was this… the prophecy. That I would bring disaster to the kingdom."

His voice trembled, not with weakness, but with the raw edge of betrayal. "I saw it, Father. In the city. The monsters tore through the market like reapers in a field. Innocent people died because of me. They wouldn't touch me, but they devoured everything around me. Women, children, anything that moved. Their blood is on my hands, and you knew."

Gorgo's face crumpled, a sob escaping her. She reached out, fingers trembling, but Mydei stepped back even if his heart ripped at his own action, the distance between them vast as an ocean.

Eurypon's shoulders sagged, the king's mask cracking to reveal the weary father beneath. 

"We only wanted to protect you," he murmured, voice thick. "The seers spoke of it at your birth. We thought... if we sent you away when you were old enough and hid the truth, you could live free of it. Soften your edges, find peace among the common folk. But it seems… the shadows have followed anyway."

Mydei laughed, a bitter, hollow sound that echoed off the walls. "Peace? I found more than that… but it doesn't matter now."

He straightened, resolve hardening his features. "I've come to end it. I'll offer my life to the ancient altar in the temple. Draw the beasts there, let them take me. The prophecy demands disaster from the prince of Castrum Kremnos. If I'm gone, the kingdom lives."

Gorgo's breath hitched, her composure shattering.

"No," she whispered, shaking her head as tears spilled down her cheeks. "My boy... You can't—"

At Mydei’s decisive and flaring glare, she could only turn away, hand clutching her chest, unable to bear the weight of his words. With a choked sob, she fled the room, her footsteps fading into the corridors like a retreating storm, leaving only the echo of a mother's breaking heart.

Eurypon watched her go, his own eyes glistening, sorrow carving deep furrows in his brow.

He approached Mydei then, placing a heavy hand on his shoulder.

"If this is your choice... I accept it, for the kingdom’s sake. But know this, my son… I am proud of the man you've become." His voice broke on the last words, but he nodded, the king's duty overriding the father's grief.

Mydei nodded once, the finality of it settling like lead in his chest.

He turned and left the throne room, the guards trailing him to his old chambers, a room unchanged since his exile, with dust motes dancing in the fading light, tapestries faded but familiar.

The door closed behind him with a soft, final click, and the sound struck him like the closing of a tomb. Mydei stood motionless in the centre of the room, spear still in his hand, as though he had forgotten how to set it down.

Only when his fingers began to tremble did he lean the weapon against the wall. It slid an inch with a faint scrape and settled, the polished ash-wood shaft catching the lamplight like a silent, loyal dog that knew its master was about to die.

Then the silence truly fell.

He had expected memories of this chamber to assault him: the boy he had been, practising footwork on the rug, sneaking sweets from the golden box on the dresser, listening at the door for his mother’s footsteps.

But the room felt alien now, a museum of someone else’s childhood. The hyacinth scent was faint and stale, the tapestries moth-eaten. Everything smelled of dust and endings.

He moved to the bed as though wading through deep water and sat on the very edge, spine straight, hands open on his thighs like a penitent. For a long time he simply breathed, counting heartbeats, trying to keep the images at bay.

He failed; they came anyway, vivid and merciless.

Phainon leaning in the farmhouse doorway at dawn, silver hair tousled, steam curling from the mug in his hand. The crooked, sleepy smile that had unravelled Mydei more surely than any battlefield victory ever had.

Phainon’s rough palms sliding up his bare back in the bed, their essence slick between their bodies, mouth hot against his ear whispering Mydei, Mydei, like the name itself was something sacred.

Phainon above him in the dark, blue eyes fierce with reverence, voice cracking on the words “You are beautiful”, as Mydei shattered and was remade in the same breath.

He pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes until sparks burst behind the lids, but the pictures only sharpened.

He saw the kitchen table set for two, pomegranate arils gleaming like drops of blood in the wooden bowl, milk swirling pink in the clay cups. Phainon’s teasing laugh when Mydei stole the sweetest piece and licked the juice from his own fingers just to watch those blue eyes darken.

He saw autumns that would never come: the two of them turning fallen leaves into another competition, bickering and laughing until one tackled the other into a riot of red and gold.

Winters with the hearth blazing, Phainon’s arms around him from behind, chin hooked over his shoulder, murmuring nonsense about the snow on the orchard buds.

Springs when the trees would burst into blossom again and Phainon would tug him beneath the branches and kiss him until the petals rained down like blessings.

He saw himself growing old, hair threaded with silver, hands scarred from honest work instead of war, waking every morning to the same steady heartbeat beside him. Phainon’s voice, older, still saying good morning, gentle like it was the first time.

All of it gone, snatched away before it had even begun.

A wounded sound escaped him, but he didn’t recognise it as his own.

The first tear slipped free, shocking in its heat. He dashed it away with the heel of his hand, furious. Princes did not cry, nor did warriors.  But the second tear followed the path of the first, and the third, and then the dam broke entirely.

He bent forward, elbows on knees, fingers knotted so tightly in his own hair that it hurt. The sobs were silent at first, then not silent at all. They tore out of him in raw, ragged gasps, each one dragging another memory behind it like a hook through the ribs.

Phainon’s thumb brushing pomegranate juice from his lower lip.

Phainon’s low laugh when Mydei pretended to hate being carried to bed.

Phainon’s voice in the dark, fierce and certain: “You are the best thing that has ever happened to me.”

“I wanted it,” Mydei whispered to the empty room, voice splintered. “I wanted all of it. I wanted to wake up tomorrow and every tomorrow after that with you. I wanted to be yours.”

The confession broke something open inside his chest.

He curled forward until his forehead pressed against his own knees, arms wrapped around his head as though he could physically hold himself together. Tears soaked the fine linen of his trousers, but he didn’t care.

The grief that came in his throat tasted like salt and iron and the ghost of pomegranate milk.

“I’m sorry,” he choked, rocking slightly. “I’m sorry I ran. I’m sorry I didn’t trust you with the whole truth. I’m sorry I’m too late. I just…”

He lifted his head at last, eyes swollen, face wet, and stared at the window where the sky was already beginning to pale. In a few days the priests would come after him. They would dress him in white, lead him barefoot across the city he had doomed, lay him on cold stone and open his veins for the kingdom’s salvation.

“Phainon,” he said aloud, the name a sob and a prayer and a goodbye all at once.

They wouldn't be together. Not in this life, at least.

But perhaps, in ending it all, he could give Phainon peace —a world without the shadows that followed Mydei like a plague.

Dawn would come soon enough. And with it, the end.
