The farmhouse had never felt so large.

Phainon had lived in it all his life, twenty-seven harvests, and it had always been just enough: one bed, one table, one door that opened onto the orchard he loved. 

Now every corner echoed.

The bed was a continent of cold linen; the chair opposite him at the table gaped like an open wound. He left the pomegranate juice untouched because the scent of it made his chest cave in.

He slept with Mydei’s discarded undershirt clutched against his face like a child with a blanket, breathing in the faint trace of sweat and sun and the ghost of that sharp, sweet skin. 

Five nights. Six mornings of waking to the same hollow silence, the same crushing certainty that the only person who had ever truly seen him was gone.

On the seventh day he could bear it no longer.

He packed light: a waterskin, hard bread, some figs and pomegranates, a wedge of cheese and the shirt that still carried Mydei’s scent. He saddled the bay gelding, pressed his forehead to the horse’s warm neck for one trembling moment, and rode north.

The road to Castrum Kremnos was longer than any he had ever travelled. He followed the river of refugees moving the opposite way, hollow-eyed families dragging carts, children clutching rag dolls, old men muttering about the prince who walked with death at his heels. 

Each time the name “Mydeimos” was spoken, Phainon’s heart lurched so violently he had to grip the reins until his knuckles blanched.

He rode through villages that had once sent him grain and wool; now shutters were barred when they saw a lone rider, and dogs snarled at his shadow. At night he slept beneath hedgerows, waking every hour to stare at the stars and whisper the name he had only been allowed to taste once.

Mydei.

Mydei.

Mydei.

A prayer and a wound.

On the eighth dawn the land began to rise, and the white walls of the capital appeared on the horizon like the bones of some great beast bleached by the sun.

Castrum Kremnos. Mydei’s home.

Phainon slowed his horse to a walk and simply looked, letting the sight sink into him the way drought-parched earth drinks the first rain. He had imagined it a hundred times in the dark: marble and gold, banners snapping in the wind, fountains singing in courtyards.

The truth was both grander and more broken than any dream.

The outer walls were scarred black where shadow-beasts had clawed at them; siege ladders still leaned drunkenly against the stone. Yet above the damage, the city rose in tiers of blinding white, colonnades and domes catching the afternoon light like polished mother-of-pearl.

Cypress trees lined the roads like silent watchers, their dark needles shivering in the breeze. From the highest hill, the royal palace rose in layered red roofs and gold-bright trim catching the light, the great bronze gates wide open because the guards had no strength left to close them.

The smell reached him first: woodsmoke, blood, fear, and underneath it all the salt-sweet breath of the sea that curled around the city’s eastern flank. Then the sound: a low, ceaseless murmur of thousands of voices raised in grief and anger and prayer. And everywhere, the banners of the royal house, crimson and gold, hung at half-mast, torn, fluttering like dying wings.

This was where Mydei had been born.

These were the streets his feet had learned to walk.

These were the people who had once cheered him and now spat at the mention of his name.

Phainon’s throat closed. He urged the gelding forward.

The lower gate was clogged with refugees. Guards in dented breastplates tried to keep order, but when they saw a lone farmer on a mud-splashed horse they waved him through with exhausted indifference.

Phainon entered the city the way a man steps into a fever dream.

The outer ring was a warren of narrow lanes, whitewashed walls now streaked with soot and claw marks. Laundry lines sagged overhead like broken spiderwebs. Children peered from doorways with huge, silent eyes. 

Phainon’s stomach turned, but he kept moving.

He passed through the merchants’ quarter —stalls overturned, spices ground into the dust, bolts of silk shredded like bright entrails. A fountain that should have sung with clear water now ran red-brown; someone had tried to wash blood from the marble and only smeared it further.

The air reeked of iron and rotting fruit. Everywhere he looked, people moved like sleepwalkers, carrying bundles, dragging the old and the wounded toward the upper city where the palace offered what little shelter remained.

Higher he climbed, past the marble colonnades of the middle terraces where once philosophers had argued and lovers had strolled. Now the pillars were cracked, statues toppled, their stone faces shattered.

A temple to the Strife Titan had lost its roof; inside, families huddled around a tiny fire, sharing a single loaf. One of them, an old man with a white beard, lifted his head as Phainon passed.

His eyes were glassy, fixed on nothing at all. “He’s come back to kill us all,” he whispered, voice hollow. “The prince will bleed. Then maybe the shadows will leave.”

Phainon’s hands shook on the reins.

He crested the final hill as the sun bled gold across the palace. The great bronze gates stood open, guarded by soldiers whose eyes were hollow with sleeplessness. Beyond them lay the courtyard of the royal house: a sweep of white marble veined with lapis, ringed by lemon trees in terracotta pots.

Once it would have been fragrant and cool. Now, the trees were scorched, the fountain dry, and the marble was littered with broken spears and torn banners. In the center stood the ancient altar of the kingdom’s founding: a slab of black stone veined with silver, stained darker still by centuries of offerings, where Mydei would lie upon to sacrifice himself.

Phainon dismounted. His legs nearly buckled. The palace rose above him in tiers of arches and balconies, its walls painted with fading frescoes of heroes and gods.

Somewhere inside those walls Mydei was breathing, hurting, believing himself alone. Phainon’s chest ached so fiercely he pressed a fist to it, as though he could hold his heart together by force.

A young guard, barely more than a boy, approached warily. “State your business.”

Phainon’s voice came out rough, scraped raw by days of silence and unshed tears. “I’ve come for the crown prince.”

The boy’s eyes widened. “No one sees him. King’s orders. He—”

“I know,” Phainon cut in, soft but unyielding. “I’m just what he left behind. Tell him Phainon is here.”

The guard hesitated, then turned and ran.

Phainon stood in the courtyard as the sun sank lower, painting the palace blood-red. Around him the city held its breath; ten thousand souls waiting for a sacrifice that would come too fast.

He could feel their fear, their hatred, their desperate hope pressing against his skin like a storm about to break.

He did not care.

Let them hate and fear. Let the whole world burn at his feet.

He had crossed half a kingdom on a half-mad horse, slept on cold ground, eaten nothing but grief for seven days, because somewhere behind those walls was the sharp-tongued, fierce-hearted man who had looked at a simple farmer and said, “I want you, all of you.”

Phainon would walk through fire, through every shadow the prophecy could spit at him, to keep the vow he had made in the dark of a farmhouse bed, spoken while his lover slept, unaware of his longlasting promise:

“I will love you for the rest of my life.”

And no crown, no curse, no altar in the world would take Mydei from him before that promise was kept.

The priests came for him before the sun had even risen. They moved like ghosts in the half-light, scarlet robes brushing the floor without a sound.

Mydei had been sitting on the edge of the bed for hours, fully dressed already, waiting. When the door opened he rose without a word. Silence was a mercy; he had no voice left for anything else.

The white linen robe slid over his shoulders like cool water, weightless and cold. It clung to his skin the way Phainon’s warm hands once had, and the contrast made the cloth feel colder than nakedness.

The hem whispered against his bare ankles with every step, a constant, soft reminder: this was the garment of the dead. They bound his wrists with silk the colour of dried blood. The knot was ceremonial, loose enough that he could have slipped free with a twist of his fingers. They knew he would not. 

Mydei felt the silk settle against his pulse and thought, absurdly, of the way Phainon used to tie his hair back with a strip of cloth when they worked the orchard —rough fingers brushing the nape of his neck, breath warm against his ear. The memory was so vivid he almost staggered.

He walked barefoot.

The marble was ice beneath his soles. Each footstep sounded too loud in the hush, like a heartbeat that had already decided to stop. Torches guttered in their sconces, throwing long, wavering shadows that reached for him and fell short.

The corridors stretched endlessly, the same corridors he had run through as a child, laughing, barefoot then too but for very different reasons.

He passed the little alcove behind the tapestry where he used to hide when lessons became unbearable, a secret hollow barely large enough for a boy and his dreams. He remembered pressing his back to the cool stone, counting heartbeats until the tutors gave up, pretending the darkness was a fortress that belonged only to him.

Now the darkness belonged to no one, and the fortress was inside his chest: a perfect, scooped-out chamber where hope had lived for one brief, blazing season. 

The void did not hurt anymore; it simply was. A quiet, tideless sea; he floated on it.

Halfway down the eastern gallery, the air changed.

A breath of warmth drifted past him, carrying the scent of crushed pomegranate and sun-warmed hay, the ghost of an orchard that no longer had any claim on him. It felt so real that Mydei stopped walking entirely. The priests halted two paces ahead, uncertain.

He closed his eyes and inhaled, slow and deliberate, letting the scent flood his lungs the way Phainon’s kisses once had.

For one heartbeat the corridor vanished. He was standing in the kitchen doorway again, dawn light spilling across the table, Phainon turning with a sleepy smile, holding out a mug swirled pink with milk and pomegranate juice.

His bound hands lifted of their own accord, reaching for a warmth that was not there. The silk cords brushed his cheek like a lover’s knuckles.

The scent faded as quickly as it had come.

He opened his eyes. The corridor was cold again, the torches guttering, the priests waiting. Only the ache behind his ribs remained, sharper now, edged with the cruel precision of a blade that knew exactly where to cut. His mind, merciless, supplied the rest.

He saw Phainon’s hands cracking pomegranates open over a wooden bowl, juice running ruby between strong fingers. Heard the low, teasing laugh when Mydei stole a piece and the juice stained his mouth red.

Felt phantom arms sliding around his waist from behind, a chin hooking over his shoulder, a murmured “I’ve got you” that had once been enough to make the entire world fall away.

He understood, with a clarity that felt like dying, that the scent had not been a kindness. It was a farewell his own heart had manufactured because it could not bear a real one.

Mydei lowered his hands.

The priests resumed walking. He followed, barefoot, white-robed, hollowed out and perfectly quiet, carrying the ghost of a familiar orchard inside him all the way to the altar where the rest of him would soon be offered up.

They had cleared the processional way. Ten thousand people stood shoulder to shoulder, yet no one made a sound. Some held their children up so they could see the prince who would die to save them; some wept openly, and some stared with the blank hatred of people who have lost everything and needed someone to blame.

Mydei felt every gaze the way a condemned man feels the weight of the noose before it is placed around his neck.

He reached the courtyard.

The altar waited exactly as it had waited for every royal sacrifice in a thousand years: black stone veined with silver, still wet from the libation poured at moonrise. Dawn had broken already; the rays of sun struck the stone and turned the wetness to fresh blood.

Mydei climbed the three shallow steps alone and knelt.

The high priest began the invocation in old kremnoan, voice rolling like distant thunder. Mydei heard none of it. He was listening for something else —a voice that would never again say his name the way only one man ever had.

The ceremonial dagger was placed in his bound hands. Light. Almost weightless. Meant for his own throat. He curled his fingers around the hilt and waited for the beasts to come. They always came when royal blood was offered.

He closed his eyes and then felt the world tilt.

A breath, warm and real, ghosted across his lips. Then another. Then the impossible pressure of a mouth he had kissed a hundred times in dreams and in life far fewer than he wished.

He thought: I have finally gone mad. Good… let madness be kinder than waking.

But the mouth moved against his, desperate, familiar, alive, and a voice he had mourned until his throat bled spoke one trembling inch from his own.

“I told you I wouldn’t leave you. Did you think I was lying?”

Mydei’s eyes flew open. Phainon was there, in front him. Dust-streaked, silver hair wild, shirt torn at the shoulder, blue eyes red-rimmed and blazing with something fiercer than sunrise.

He had forced his way past the ring of priests, vaulted the barrier, and now knelt behind Mydei on the altar itself, arms locked around his waist as though he could anchor him to the earth by sheer will.

The courtyard exploded into chaos: shouts, drawn steel, the high priest’s staff clattering to the stones; but Mydei heard none of it. There was only Phainon’s heartbeat hammering against his spine, Phainon’s hands trembling where they cradled his face, Phainon’s voice cracking on every word.

“Look at me,” Phainon whispered, fierce and pleading. “Look at me, Mydei. I am here.”

Mydei’s bound hands came up slowly, helplessly, until his fingertips brushed Phainon’s cheek, rough with stubble, wet with tears that were not his own.

“You came,” he breathed, the words barely sound. “You… came.”

Phainon laughed, a broken, incredulous thing. “You thought I wouldn’t? You thought I would wake up every morning for the rest of my life without you and just… accept it?”

His thumbs wiped the tears sliding down Mydei’s face, over and over, as though he could erase the night itself. “I still taste you on my tongue every time I drink pomegranate. I still reach for you in the dark and find cold sheets. I am half a man without you, Mydei. Do you understand that?”

Mydei’s voice shattered. “But the prophecy—”

“Listen to me.” Phainon’s grip tightened, not letting him look away. “The prophecy says the prince of Castrum Kremnos will bring disaster. Then you should just stop being the prince.”

A hush fell, so complete that even the wind seemed to still.

Phainon dropped to one knee on the blood-stained altar, right there in front of a king and queen and ten thousand witnesses, and took Mydei’s bound hands between his own calloused ones.

“I love you,” he said, loud enough for the whole city to hear, soft enough that only Mydei felt the tremor in it.

“I love you on your worst day and on your best day, and on every day in between. I love the way you blush when I tease you. I love the way you steal the sweetest pomegranate and pretend it was a coincidence. I love the way you say my name when you’re falling apart under me. I love you when you are a prince, and I love you when you are only Mydei.”

He pressed his forehead to Mydei’s, tears falling freely now.

“Come home,” he whispered, the same words he had wished to say since the day he left him. “Leave the crown. Leave the name they forced on you. Let them keep their disaster. I only want you. Just you.” Phainon didn’t stop once, words flowing out like a wound finally allowed to bleed. “Marry me, Mydei. Let the orchard be our kingdom, the farmhouse our palace and our bed the only throne we’ll ever need.”

Mydei was crying so hard he could barely see, the void inside him suddenly, violently full —full of Phainon’s voice, warmth, Phainon’s impossible, stubborn, devoted love.

He looked past Phainon’s shoulder to where his parents stood, rigid and pale. Gorgo’s eyes were wet, and Eurypon inclined his head once, signaling what Mydei now most wanted from him: Permission and forgiveness.

Mydei let the crimson silk slip from his wrists. He looked back at the man kneeling in front of him and spoke the words he had never dared believe he would get to say.

“Take me home, Phainon.”

Phainon’s smile broke across his face like dawn after the longest night. He rose, pulled Mydei to his feet, and kissed him slowly in front of the entire capital. No shame nor hesitation. Only a promise.

Behind them, the shadow-beasts that had begun to gather at the edges of the city wavered, frayed, and melted into nothing.

The prophecy had demanded the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.

It had not imagined the prince would choose, freely and finally, to stop being one.

Years later, old men in the rebuilt city would swear that on the morning the prince vanished, the sky itself sighed in relief, and every pomegranate tree in the kingdom burst into blossom out of season.

And far away to the south, in a small farmhouse, silver and golden heads would sit on their porch at dusk, sharing a single clay cup of milk and pomegranate juice, fingers laced, whispering to each other the oath the fates could never cut loose:

“I choose you. Always.”
